subject: chemistry
title: Atomic structure and isotopes
key_idea: An atom has a small, dense **nucleus** of protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells around it. The **atomic number** is the number of protons, and it identifies the element. **Isotopes** are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.

blocks.text: An atom is made of three sub-atomic particles. This section covers where they are, their relative masses and charges, and how mass and charge are spread out.

items.meaning: The very small, dense centre of the atom. It contains the protons and neutrons.
A region of space around the nucleus where electrons are found.
The mass of a particle compared with the mass of a proton, which is taken as 1.
The charge of a particle compared with the charge of a proton, which is taken as +1.

blocks.text: How mass and charge are distributed

items: The atom is **mostly empty space**. The nucleus is tiny compared with the whole atom.
Almost all the mass is in the nucleus, because protons and neutrons are about 1836 times heavier than an electron.
All the positive charge is in the nucleus, from the protons. The negative charge is spread through the space around it, from the electrons.
An atom is neutral overall: it has the same number of protons and electrons.
Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus. Electrons are in shells around it.
Proton: mass 1, charge +1. Neutron: mass 1, charge 0. Electron: mass 1/1836, charge −1.
Nearly all of the mass is in the nucleus, and nearly all of the volume is empty space.

sections.heading: How ideas about the atom changed

blocks.text: The model of the atom has changed as new evidence appeared. A model is accepted while it explains the evidence, and replaced when it cannot.

rows: A tiny, solid ball that cannot be split.
Electrons were discovered, so atoms have smaller parts.
Negative electrons spread through a ball of positive charge.
Alpha particles fired at gold foil: a few were deflected by large angles, and some bounced back.
A tiny positive nucleus, with electrons around it in mostly empty space.
Atoms give line spectra and ionisation energies, which need electrons at fixed energies.
Electrons in fixed shells, each with its own energy.
Quantum theory showed shells are made of sub-shells and orbitals.

items: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, so atoms are mostly empty space.
A few were deflected strongly, so the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a small nucleus.
The Bohr model explains periodic properties, such as the repeating pattern in ionisation energies, because shells fill in order.
Models are changed or rejected when new evidence does not fit them.
Scattering of alpha particles gave evidence for a small, dense, positive nucleus.
The Bohr model of electron shells explains periodic properties.

sections.heading: Counting particles in atoms and ions

blocks.text: Two numbers identify an atom. From them, and the charge, you can work out how many of each particle there are.

items.meaning: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It decides which element the atom is.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

blocks.label: Number of neutrons
blocks.formula: number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number

items: **Protons** = atomic number. This never changes for an element.
**Neutrons** = A − Z.
**Electrons** in an atom = Z. In an ion, electrons = Z − charge. A positive ion has lost electrons. A negative ion has gained them.
For a molecule or a molecular ion, add up the particles of each atom, then adjust the electrons for any charge.

items.text: The Al³⁺ ion in ²⁷₁₃Al³⁺ has A = 27 and Z = 13, and a charge of +3.
13 − 3 = 10, because the 3+ ion has lost three electrons.

diagram.alt: A practice question: find the number of electrons in an ion from its atomic number, mass number and charge.
diagram.question: A positive ion has mass number {A}, atomic number {Z} and a charge of {q}+. How many electrons does it have?
working: Electrons in the atom = atomic number = {Z}.
The ion has lost {q} electrons, so electrons = {Z} − {q} = {answer}.

items: Protons = Z. Neutrons = A − Z. Electrons = Z − charge.
The number of protons decides the element. The number of electrons decides the charge.

blocks.text: Atoms of one element are not all identical. This section covers what isotopes are, how they are written and how their properties compare.

items.meaning: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers.

blocks.text: An isotope is written with its mass number at the top left and its atomic number at the bottom left, for example ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C. Both have 6 protons.

diagram.alt: A comparison of two chlorine isotopes: chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 have the same protons and electrons, but 18 and 20 neutrons.
items: ³⁵₁₇Cl
³⁷₁₇Cl
Isotopes of an element have the **same chemical properties**. Chemical reactions depend on the electrons, and isotopes have the same number of electrons in the same arrangement.
Neutrons have no charge, so they do not change how the atom reacts.
Isotopes have **different physical properties**, such as mass and density, because more neutrons mean a greater mass.
Properties that depend on mass also differ, such as the rate of diffusion of a gas.
Isotopes: same number of protons, different number of neutrons.
Same electron arrangement, so the same chemical properties.
Different mass, so different physical properties such as density.

checks.q: State the relative mass and relative charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
checks.a: Proton: mass 1, charge +1. Neutron: mass 1, charge 0. Electron: mass 1/1836 (or negligible), charge −1.

checks.q: A sulfide ion, ³²₁₆S²⁻, is formed. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in it.
Explain why ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl have the same chemical properties but different densities.
checks.a: They have the same number of electrons, in the same arrangement, so they react in the same way. ³⁷Cl has two more neutrons, so its atoms have a greater mass and a greater density.

blocks.text: A mass spectrometer is the instrument that shows isotopes directly. The next note covers it in full; here is the outline.

items: A time of flight instrument has five stages: ionisation, acceleration to give all ions the same kinetic energy, ion drift, ion detection and data analysis.
It gives accurate relative isotopic masses and the relative abundance of each isotope.
A spectrum of an element has one peak per isotope, so it can identify the element. A molecule's heaviest peak gives its relative molecular mass.
Mass spectrometry measures isotope masses and abundances.
It can identify elements and find relative molecular mass.

blocks.text: Protons, neutrons and electrons moving at the same velocity can be sent through an electric field between two charged plates. Their paths show their charge and mass.

items: **Protons** are positive, so they bend towards the negative plate.
**Electrons** are negative, so they bend towards the positive plate.
**Neutrons** have no charge, so they go straight on and are not deflected.
The electron beam bends further than the proton beam. The charges are equal in size, but an electron is about 1836 times lighter, so it is deflected much more.

blocks.text: The notation ˣ_yA gives the mass number x at the top and the atomic number y at the bottom, as in ¹⁴₆C. Isotopes of one element share y but have different x.

items: In an electric field: protons towards negative, electrons towards positive, neutrons undeflected.
The electron is deflected more because it has far less mass for the same size of charge.
